newsitem.title: UK: Spurt in UK M4 flashes warning light on inflation.
newsitem.headline: Spurt in UK M4 flashes warning light on inflation.

text.p: A spurt in UK broad money growth in September combines with other recent data to suggest the inflation outlook is deteriorating and promises to make the Bank of England even more keen to raise interest rates.

"This rise, coming with other data showing the economy is moving up one or two gears, will make the Bank of England even more twitchy about tightening monetary policy," said Philip Shaw, group economist at Union Plc. M4 growth accelerated to 9.8 percent in September from 9.5 in August. The monthly rise in September was 0.8 percent.
M4 year-on-year growth has been above the 9.0 percent upper limit of the government's monitoring range for almost a year.
Some of the sharp acceleration has been prompted by frenetic corporate activity, especially in the financial sector.
And the September figures were boosted by the higher-than- expected PSBR, swollen by a 1.2 billion stg debt payment from the inflation uplift on a redeemed index-linked gilt.
"Stripping out the erratic public sector element, the underlying picture is weaker-than-expected with M4 lending to the private sector lower," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
M4 lending was 3.5 billion stg in September, compared with 5.4 billion in August, and the weakest figure since August last year.
But Loynes concedes it is too early to say M4 is slowing. "And as long as it holds above the monitoring range, the Bank of England will point to it as a reason to hike rates."
In its last inflation report the Bank said the continued strength of M4 was inconsistent with the tough 2.5 percent inflation target.
The Bank has already made it clear it wants to see interest rates back up at 6.0 percent from 5.75 percent.
But M4 figures, along with other strong data this month, may prompt Governor Eddie George to up the ante at the next monetary meeting and call for a full 50 basis point increase.

Most disappointing in the September figures was underlying inflation which edged up to 2.9 percent having spent four months stuck at 2.8 percent. And latest earnings data were an unpleasant surprise. The ONS revised up July average earnings to 4.0 percent in July and they stuck there in August.
Many economists have recently revised up their RPIX forecasts and the latest summary of independent forecasts from the Treasury showed the average forecast higher at 2.9 percent.
This compares with 2.8 percent last month. The average RPIX forecast for 1996 also edged up, to 2.7 percent from 2.6 percent.
Other figures released on Friday showed the recovery in the housing market continued unabated in September.

Net new approvals stood at 3.717 billion stg compared with 3.66 billion stg in August. "Mortgage demand continues to grow at a robust pace and should ensure house prices continue to rise over the winter months," said Loynes.
Adrian Coles, director-general of the Building Societies Association, said the strength of the housing market recovery is clear.
"The recovery is well established, but there may be some fluctuations from month to month."
He said while measures to help the housing market in November's budget would be welcome, "the overriding aim should be for economic stability which will improve confidence and underpin the recovery."
